summary: Extends PIDF with a timed-status element so a presentity can declare its status for a period fully in the future or the past. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A calendar note that says I will be away next week, or I was out yesterday, instead of only how things are right now.

questions: how to show future presence status
what is the from attribute in timed-status
can timed-status include the present time
subtitle: A PIDF extension that lets a presentity announce its status for a time span that is entirely in the past or the future.

tldr.problem: Basic presence data only describes the present. A presentity cannot say it will be CLOSED next week, and the PIDF status element element has no way to carry a time range.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4481 adds a timed-status element to the PIDF tuple. It carries a required 'from' attribute and an optional 'until' attribute, and the range must not include the present time.
tldr.outcome: Watchers can plan around a presentity's future plans and see recent past status. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4481 is a Proposed Standard from July 2006, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The companion extensions it refers to are RFC 4480 (RPID) and RFC 4482 (CIPID).

sections.title: Why Presence Needs a Time Range
sections.content:
The Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) is a basic XML format for describing the presence of a presentity, short for presence entity, which is typically a uniquely identified person. Traditionally, PIDF and its rich extension RPID (RFC 4480) describe only the current state of the presentity.

The RFC argues that a watcher can plan better if it knows the presentity's future plans. For example, a watcher who knows the presentity is about to travel might place a phone call earlier. Past information can also help: knowing the presentity was at an off-site meeting that ended an hour ago suggests it is probably in transit now.

RPID can already say when one aspect of presence is valid, but the PIDF <status> element cannot, so there is no way to say a presentity will be OPEN or CLOSED in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Your friends usually see only what you are doing this minute. This lets you also tell them what you will be doing later, or what you were doing a little while ago.

sections.title: Why a New Element Instead of Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC explains why it does not just add time attributes to the existing <status> element. PIDF parsers that do not understand the new attributes would ignore them, and so could not tell current status from future status. A reader without the extension would treat a future CLOSED as the present.

Instead, the document defines a separate <timed-status> element for status that is either no longer valid or covers a future period. Old parsers simply do not see it as the current status.

The extension also chose absolute times rather than relative ones, because relative times would be too hard to keep properly updated when spacing notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: If you scribbled a date on an old sign, someone who could not read the scribble would think the sign was current. A separate new sign avoids the mix-up.

sections.title: The timed-status Element
sections.content:
The <timed-status> element is a child of the PIDF <tuple>. It MUST NOT appear inside a PIDF <status> element or inside another <timed-status>. More than one may appear in a tuple.

It MUST carry a from attribute and MAY carry an until attribute. They give the time the status took on this value and the time until which it is expected to be valid. Without until, the information is assumed valid until the tuple is explicitly overridden or expires under the publication mechanism in use.

Inside the element can sit <basic> and <note>, plus any other element that suits a PIDF status extension and has a limited validity period. The PIDF-LO location extensions (RFC 4119) are given as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note says when it starts and, if you want, when it ends. Inside it you write the status, like open or closed, and maybe a little message.

sections.title: Rules for Time Ranges and Overlaps
sections.content:
The time range MUST NOT encompass the present time, meaning the PIDF <timestamp> value. Otherwise it would offer an unnecessary and confusing second way to describe current presence. So a <timed-status> without until must have a from that lies in the future. Originators MUST produce times fully in the past or future relative to local wallclock time and any PIDF timestamp.

Sources should avoid overlapping elements, but overlapping appointments are common in calendars, so receivers MUST be able to render overlapping indications.

While composing a document, a presence agent (PA) may find a stored <timed-status> that covers the present. It MAY discard it, or convert it to a regular <status> if it considers that information more credible.
sections.plainLanguage: A note must be about before or after now, never about right now, because right now already has its own place. If two calendar entries overlap, the viewer must still be able to show both.

sections.title: An Example Document
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a PIDF document for pres:someone@example.com. The tuple has a normal <status> with <basic>open</basic>, so the person is open now. A <ts:timed-status> with from 2005-08-15T10:20:00.000-05:00 and until 2005-08-22T19:30:00.000-05:00 contains <ts:basic>closed</ts:basic>. The presence document's own note says "I'll be in Tokyo next week".

Read together: open today, closed for the week ahead.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the sign says open. A second sign says closed from one Monday to the next, and a note explains the person is traveling.

sections.title: XML Schema and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The schema defines timed-status in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:timed-status. Its content is an optional basic, an optional note, and any number of elements from other namespaces. The from attribute is required and typed as an XML Schema dateTime; until is optional with the same type.

IANA is asked to register that namespace URN and the schema, following the IETF XML Registry (RFC 3688). The registrant contact is the IETF SIMPLE working group, and the schema registrant is the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are written in a strict form computers can check, and the name of the extension is put on an official list so nobody else uses it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's whole security section is one sentence: the security issues are similar to those for RPID (RFC 4480). It adds no mechanisms of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: This note has the same safety worries as the other presence add-ons, so the authors point there instead of repeating them.
